# The window is told, not asked

> A screen that polls is stale for as long as its interval, and the interval is a guess about how impatient the reader is; watching the logs is exact, and it turns out to cost nothing because the logs are always a host path.

Applies to `app/src-tauri/src`, `web/src/core`.

<!-- archwarden:yours -->

## Context

_Everything between these two markers is yours. archwarden never rewrites it._

<!-- archwarden:end -->

## Considered and rejected

- **Polling, on a short interval** (nothing refuses it) — What shipped, at ten seconds, with `for now` written beside it. Every reader waits up to the interval for a change that already happened, and each poll runs `git diff` on every open project whether anything moved or not.
- **`Runtime::watch`, so a runtime watches its own tree** (nothing refuses it) — The architecture's hard rule 3 names it and it is not needed: `configDir` is written in this machine's spelling by definition — it is how the logs are read at all — so the logs of a VM, a container or an ssh host are already a local path. The harder problem was anticipated than the one that exists.
- **An event carrying what changed** (nothing refuses it) — A filesystem event says a line landed in some log, which is not a fact any screen is shaped around. A payload naming a path would invite a screen to believe it knows which of its questions went stale, and be wrong the first time two things moved at once.
- **Falling back to polling in silence** (nothing refuses it) — A window that looks live while it is a minute behind lies with more confidence than one that admits it. The same argument `RuntimeError::Unsupported` already makes about a watch that reports nothing.

## What keeps it

Nothing can. Whether a screen listens or polls is behaviour. A rule can see that `setInterval` exists, not that it is a fallback rather than the mechanism — and the fallback is deliberate, so a rule forbidding the call would forbid the right code.
